title: Chanted in Myanmar
hookLine: Abhidhamma is chanted at funerals and studied by lay people in Myanmar

cards: Evening, in a house in Myanmar. Someone in the family has died. Neighbors have come, and monks sit at the front of the room.
Then the chanting begins, steady and low, in Pali. If you followed the words, you might expect something about grief, or heaven, or the person who's gone.

Instead you'd hear lists: states of mind, kinds of conditions, the same lists this path has walked through for weeks, the ones that can look dry as a dictionary on the page. Here they're sung, over someone who has died.

teach.b: First, what's being chanted. The first book of the Abhidhamma opens with three short phrases. In Pali: kusala dhamma, akusala dhamma, abyakata dhamma.
Wholesome states, unwholesome states, and states that are neither. That's how the higher teaching begins, sorting every moment of mind into one of three kinds.

Chanted slowly, the lines have a rhythm, like a list of names read at a memorial. Second, why at a funeral. The Buddha, tradition says, taught the Abhidhamma to his mother in a heaven, over one rainy season.
Some Buddhists connect the funeral chant to that story.

teach.h: A GIFT FIRST GIVEN TO HIS MOTHER.
teach.b: The teaching was first given as a gift to someone who had died, so it's offered again, for the one just gone and the family in the room.
The chanting is also a way of making merit, and in Theravada practice merit is shared with the dead. Third, who studies it. In Myanmar the Abhidhamma isn't left only to monks.

Lay people with jobs and children study it too, in classes at the monastery, with a teacher and a printed manual open on the table, learning the same lists of factors and conditions. Fourth, what that pairing shows.
Chanted at night over the dead, studied by day at a table, the same words do two jobs.

They're something to understand, line by line, and something to hear, carried by a voice, in a room where understanding isn't the point. A list can be a map, and it can also be a sound that keeps people company.

how: In Myanmar, monks chant passages of the Abhidhamma at funerals and memorial gatherings, and lay people study its lists in classes at monasteries.

the story of the Buddha's own funeral, chanted
the Abhidhamma's lists, sung as a gift for the dead

games.why: they chant the Abhidhamma's lists: wholesome, unwholesome, neither, and on through the conditions. dry on the page, it becomes a gift in the room.

practice: If you have a recording of Pali chanting, play a short stretch quietly; if not, listen to whatever sound is in the room, a fan, traffic, your own breath.
Don't try to understand it; let the sound arrive and pass, the way the chanted lists roll on, phrase after phrase. If someone you've lost comes to mind, let them sit in the sound with you.
